knowledge_point.title: Transforming First-Order Linear ODEs Using Integrating Factors

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y = y(x)$:
$\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{11}{3}\right)\cdot y=\cos{\left(3 x \right)}$
Write the equation in the form $\frac{d}{dx}(yI(x)) = I(x)Q(x)$, where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{11}{3}$ and $Q(x)=\cos{\left(3 x \right)}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\int \left(\frac{11}{3}\right)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\frac{11 x}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=e^{\frac{11 x}{3}}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x)\cdot \left(\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{11}{3}\right)\cdot y\right) & =I(x)\cdot \left(\cos{\left(3 x \right)}\right) \\ I(x)\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)I(x)y & =\left(e^{\frac{11 x}{3}}\right)\cdot \left(\cos{\left(3 x \right)}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot \left(e^{\frac{11 x}{3}}\right)\right) & =\left(e^{\frac{11 x}{3}}\right)\cdot \left(\cos{\left(3 x \right)}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-5$ and $Q(x)=3{e}^{3x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int -5\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-5x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-5x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-5y) & ={e}^{-5x}\cdot 3{e}^{3x} \\ {e}^{-5x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-5{e}^{-5x}\cdot y & =3{e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-5x}) & =3{e}^{-2x} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-5x})\text{d}x & =\int 3{e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{-5x} & =-\frac{3{e}^{-2x}}{2}+C \\ y & =-\frac{3{e}^{3x}}{2}+C{e}^{5x}\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{5}y=\frac{2x}{5}
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{5}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{2x}{5}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 1/5\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x/5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{x/5}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/5}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{5}y) & ={e}^{x/5}\cdot \frac{2x}{5} \\ {e}^{x/5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{5}{e}^{x/5}\cdot y & =\frac{2x}{5}{e}^{x/5}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x/5}) & =\frac{2x}{5}{e}^{x/5} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x/5})\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2x}{5}{e}^{x/5}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem:

An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x) =$ {{field-1}}.

The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x) =$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=1.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int 1\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=e^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+1y) & =e^{x}\cdot 1 \\ e^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+e^{x}y & =e^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{x}) & =e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ye^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int e^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ ye^{x} & =1\left(1 e^{x}\right)+C \\ ye^{x} & =e^{x}+C \\ y & =\left(C + e^{x}\right) e^{- x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=7$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =\frac{(e^{(0)})+C}{(e^{(0)})} \\ 7 & =\frac{1+C}{1} \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=1 + 6 e^{- x}.
$$
